content:
Hong Kong recorded record-breaking high temperatures in August, with the elderly and vulnerable groups bearing the brunt. Greenpeace today (the 24th) released the "Elderly Heat Risk Assessment and Community Support Survey," which showed that 35% of elderly respondents said they "never" or "rarely" turned on air conditioning during hot weather, with the proportion exceeding 50% among those living in subdivided flats, rooftop houses, or old tenement buildings. Nearly 80% of surveyed elderly had experienced discomfort due to high temperatures, with mood and sleep also affected, and 5.5% had been hospitalised as a result. Nearly 70% of the elderly mistakenly believed that "staying at home means no risk of heatstroke." Greenpeace interviewed 127 elderly aged 65 or above in seven districts—Kwun Tong, Wong Tai Sin, Central and Western, Kowloon City, Tsuen Wan, Kwai Tsing, and Eastern—between June and July this year. Among them, 54.3% lived in public housing estates, 35.4% in subdivided flats, rooftop houses, or old tenement buildings, and single elderly persons and elderly couples accounted for 60% of the respondents.

The Greenpeace survey showed that 35% of elderly respondents said they "never" or "rarely" turned on air conditioning during hot weather.

Mistakenly believing that "staying at home means no risk of heatstroke"

The survey found that the elderly lacked awareness of heat prevention and also faced the problem of "energy poverty." Over 70% (71.6%) of the elderly underestimated the risk, mistakenly believing that "staying at home means no risk of heatstroke" or "did not know about the relevant risks." Greenpeace project officer Yeung Kit-lai pointed out that the elderly habitually considered staying indoors with a roof over their heads as safe, and coupled with the fact that their bodies were less sensitive to temperature changes, they lacked the awareness and ability to prevent heat crises, making in-home heatstroke highly likely.

Moreover, 35% of surveyed elderly said they "never" (18.9%) or "rarely" (15.7%) turned on air conditioning during hot weather; the proportion of elderly living in subdivided flats, rooftop houses, or old tenement buildings who "never" or "rarely" turned on air conditioning during hot weather exceeded 50% (55.1%), with the main reasons being lack of cooling equipment or difficulty affording high electricity bills.

Yeung said: "Electricity bills are the biggest deterrent preventing them from using air conditioning. For elderly living in inadequate housing in particular, they face an additional difficulty and challenge—landlords may overcharge for electricity. Their homes have never had suitable cooling equipment."

The survey showed that nearly 80% (78.7%) of the elderly had experienced physical discomfort due to high temperatures.

Nearly 90% of elderly have never used cooling centres

In addition, nearly 80% (78.7%) of the elderly had experienced physical discomfort due to high temperatures, and had not received any form of heat prevention support services in the past two years; as many as 95% of elderly "never" (88.2%) or "rarely used" (7.1%) cooling centres, with reasons including "not knowing the location," "not knowing cooling centres existed," or "being too far away."

In the scorching summer heat, residents prepare small portable fans to help cool down when going out.

Elderly in Wong Tai Sin must climb a long staircase to reach cooling centres

Yeung said that organisations had inspected cooling centres in Shek Kip Mei, Lam Tin, and Wong Tai Sin, finding their locations hidden and remote. For example, the Wong Tai Sin cooling centre is located south of Tsz Wan Shan on a hillside, requiring the climbing of a long slope and staircase, making it difficult for nearby elderly to use. As a result, with no alternatives, the elderly could only go to shopping malls and community living rooms. However, shopping malls have no seating for lingering, and security guards would chase people away; using community living rooms involves certain thresholds and eligibility, and in the end the elderly could only face the hot weather in shaded areas of parks.

High temperatures are the "silent killer" of the elderly

According to Department of Health data, the number of hospital discharges and deaths due to heatstroke among those aged 65 or above increased sharply from 4 to 68 between 2015 and 2024—a 16-fold increase—excluding hospital admissions for other illnesses caused by high temperatures. Yeung pointed out: "High temperatures are the 'silent killer' of the elderly. Due to declining physiological functions, some also suffer from chronic illnesses, making them a high-risk group."

Greenpeace project officer Yeung Kit-lai recommended that the government proactively provide heat prevention guidelines to the elderly and community, visit elderly who live alone or are frail, and issue summer electricity subsidies and heat relief supplies.

60% of elderly consider hot weather support insufficient

The survey indicated that nearly 60% of the elderly considered support during hot weather insufficient. Yeung said that the government currently has no clear guidelines or resource allocation to improve heat prevention support for the elderly, and can only rely on community organisations to provide limited services in individual areas. She said: "The government's current approach is effectively outsourcing the responsibility for dealing with extreme heat to civil organisations, without providing the protection due to vulnerable groups."

Organisations urge government to strengthen heat prevention support for grassroots elderly

Yeung recommended that the government proactively provide heat prevention guidelines to the elderly and community, visit elderly who live alone or are frail, and issue summer electricity subsidies and heat relief supplies; set up temporary cooling centres, strengthen publicity, and extend opening hours; and formulate a high temperature action plan as soon as possible, coordinating departments such as the Labour and Welfare Bureau and the Environment Bureau to promote climate adaptation policies and community measures supporting vulnerable groups.
